content_html:
This retirement calculator answers two questions at once: how much will you have saved when you stop working, and how much do you need to fund the retirement income you want? The difference between the two is your shortfall or surplus, and the year-by-year plan shows how long the money is likely to last.

How to use this calculator

  1. Ages: your current age, the age you plan to retire and the age to plan until. Planning a few years past your life expectancy builds in a safety margin.
  2. Income and savings: your current pre-tax income, how fast it grows, what you have saved for retirement and what share of income you save each year, including any employer contributions.
  3. Income needed in retirement: a percentage of your income just before you retire. Commuting costs, payroll taxes and retirement saving usually stop, so many people plan on 70% to 85%.
  4. Other retirement income: Social Security, a pension or rental income, entered as a yearly amount in today's dollars. Your Social Security statement at ssa.gov gives a personal estimate.
  5. Assumptions: open this section to change the return before and during retirement and the inflation rate.

How the calculation works

Before retirement, each year's savings are added at the end of the year and the balance grows at the pre-retirement return. Your income rises each year by the increase you entered.

At retirement, the yearly amount you need is your income percentage times your final income, minus your other income grown with inflation from today. That net amount is withdrawn at the start of each retirement year and increases with inflation every year, while the rest of the balance earns the return during retirement. The savings you need is the amount that would exactly fund those withdrawals until the age you plan to. If you fall short, the calculator shows the extra yearly saving that, earning the pre-retirement return, would close the gap by your retirement date.

Worked example

Take a 35-year-old earning $70,000 a year, with income rising 3% a year, $50,000 already saved and 10% of income saved each year. They plan to retire at 67, plan until age 90, want 80% of their final income, and expect $20,000 a year in today's dollars from Social Security. Returns are 6% before and 5% during retirement, with 3% inflation.

  • Savings at 67: about $1,227,607, or about $476,725 in today's dollars.
  • Income needed in the first retirement year: $144,205, of which other income covers $51,502, leaving $92,703 to come from savings.
  • Savings needed at 67 to fund that until age 90: about $1,739,709, a shortfall of about $512,102.
  • The savings would run out at about age 82. Saving roughly $5,634 more a year ($470 a month) would close the gap.

The large dollar figures reflect 32 years of income growth and inflation. The today's-dollars result is a better guide to what the money will actually buy.

Common rules of thumb

GuidelineWhat it suggests
Save 10% to 15% of incomeA typical target for someone starting in their 20s or 30s, including employer contributions
Replace 70% to 85% of incomeA rough starting point for spending in retirement
Withdraw about 4% in the first yearA first-year withdrawal rate that has historically lasted about 30 years with inflation increases

Rules of thumb are only starting points. Your own spending, health, housing costs and other income matter more than any rule.

Ways to close a shortfall

  • Save more, especially in tax-advantaged accounts such as a 401(k) or IRA, and capture any employer match.
  • Retire a little later. Each extra working year adds savings, adds growth and shortens the period the money must cover.
  • Plan to spend less in retirement, or add part-time income in the early years.
  • Delay Social Security. Benefits grow for each year you wait past full retirement age, up to age 70.

This is a simplified model. It assumes steady returns and inflation and doesn't calculate taxes on withdrawals, so treat the results as a guide rather than a forecast.

faq.question: How much do I need to retire?
faq.answer: It depends on the income you want, the other income you expect and how long retirement lasts. A common rough check is that savings of about 25 times the yearly amount you need from them supports a 4% first-year withdrawal. This calculator gives a more specific figure using your own ages, returns and inflation.

faq.question: Should the income I enter be before or after tax?
faq.answer: Enter pre-tax income. Withdrawals from traditional 401(k)s and IRAs are taxed, so a target based on pre-tax income leaves room to pay those taxes. The calculator does not work out the tax itself.

faq.question: What return should I assume?
faq.answer: No return is guaranteed. Many planners use a lower figure during retirement than before it, because portfolios usually shift toward bonds and cash as people age. Try a cautious and an optimistic case to see the range of outcomes.

faq.question: How do I include Social Security?
faq.answer: Enter your expected yearly benefit in today's dollars in the other retirement income field. Your Social Security statement at ssa.gov shows estimates for different claiming ages. The calculator raises the amount with inflation, similar to the yearly cost-of-living adjustment.

faq.question: Why does my savings run out before the age I plan to?
faq.answer: Your savings at retirement are smaller than the amount needed to fund your withdrawals for the full period. Saving more, retiring later, spending less or adding other income all push the run-out age later.
